# GL(M)Ms {#sec-glm}

::: callout-note
#### In this chapter

In this chapter, you will learn

- how a GLM connects the linear predictor to the response via a link function and a distribution, and which variant to use for which type of response (@sec-glm-variant);
- how to check GLMs with simulated residuals and fix the typical problems: overdispersion and zero-inflation (@sec-glm-residual);
- why effects and interactions depend on the scale (link vs. response scale), and how to report ratios, predictions and data-averaged effects on the response scale (@sec-glm-interaction), and what changes when you add random effects, including how to test them (@sec-glm-glmm, @sec-glm-glmmtest).

**Workflow steps** (@sec-summary): step 3 (choice of the distribution), step 5 (residual checks), step 6 (inference on the response scale).

Prerequisites: the linear model (@sec-lm), random effects (@sec-re) for the GLMM parts.
:::

## Introduction to GLMs {#sec-glm-intro}

::: {#introduction-to-glms}
:::

Generalized linear models (GLMs) extend the linear model (LM) to other (i.e. non-normal) distributions. The idea is the following:

1.  We want to keep the regression formula $y \sim f(x)$ of the lm with all its syntax, including splines (@sec-lm-gam), random effects (@sec-re) and all that. In the GLM world, this is called the "linear predictor".

2.  However, in the GLM, we now allow other residual distributions than normal, e.g. binomial, Poisson, Gamma, etc.

3.  Some families require a particular range of the predictions (e.g. binomial requires predictions between zero and one). To achieve this, we use a so-called link function to bring the results of the linear predictor to the desired range.

In R, the distribution is specified via the `family()` function, which distinguishes the glm from the lm function. If you look at the help of family, you will see that the link function is an argument of `family()`. If no link is provided, the default link for the respective family is chosen.

```{r}
?family
```

A full GLM structure is thus:

$$y \sim family[link^{-1}(f(x) + RE)]$$

::: callout-note
As you see, I noted the link function as $link^{-1}$ in this equation. The reason is that traditionally, the link function is applied to the (expected value of the) left hand side of the equation, i.e.

$$link(E[y]) = f(x)$$

This is important to keep in mind when interpreting the names of the link function - the log link, for example, means that $log(E[y]) = f(x)$, which actually means that we assume $E[y] = exp(f(x))$, i.e. the result of the linear predictor enters the exponential function, which assures that we have strictly positive predictions.
:::

The function $f(x)$ itself can have all components that we discussed before, in particular

- You can add random effects as in @sec-re-package (using functions `lme4::glmer` or `glmmTMB::glmmTMB`)

- You can also use splines using `mgcv::gam` (see @sec-lm-gam)

## Important GLM variants {#sec-glm-variant}

::: {#important-glm-variants}
:::

The most important are

- Bernoulli / Binomial family = logistic regression with logit link
- Poisson family = Poisson regression with log link
- Beta regression for continuous proportions in (0, 1)

Of course, there are many additional distributions that you could consider for your response. Here an overview of the common choices:

```{r chunk_chapter4_0, echo=FALSE, out.width="150%", out.height="150%"}
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/linkFunctions.jpg"))
```

*Screenshot taken from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model#Link_function). Content licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License 3.0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_Attribution-ShareAlike_3.0_Unported_License).*

### Count data - Poisson regression {#sec-glm-poisson}

The standard model for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, ...) is the Poisson regression, which implements

- A log-link function -\> $y = exp(ax + b)$

- A Poisson distribution

As an example, we use the data set birdfeeding from the EcoData package - the dataset consists of observations of food given by parents to nestlings as a function of the attractiveness of the nestling.

```{r}
library(EcoData)
#str(birdfeeding)
plot(feeding ~ attractiveness, data = birdfeeding)
```

To fit a Poisson regression to this data, we use the `glm()` function, specifying `family = "poisson"`. Note again that the log link function is the default (see `?family`), so it does not have to be specified.

```{r}
fit = glm(feeding ~ attractiveness, data = birdfeeding, family = "poisson")
summary(fit)
```

The output is very similar to the `lm()`, however, as the residuals are no longer assumed to scatter normally, all statistics based on R^2^ have been replaced by the deviance (defined in @nte-glm-deviance). So, we have

- Deviance residuals on top

- Instead of R^2^, we get null vs. residual deviance, and AIC. Based on the log-likelihood or the deviance, we can calculate a pseudo R^2^, e.g. McFadden, which is 1-\[LogL(M)/LogL(M~0~)\] (see the example box below)

::: {#nte-glm-deviance .callout-note}
#### Different definitions of deviance

The term *deviance* is used with two related, but different definitions, which is a common source of confusion:

1.  **Deviance of a GLM (general definition):** $D = 2\,[\log L(\text{saturated}) - \log L(\text{fitted})]$. The saturated model has one parameter per observation and fits the data (almost) perfectly, so $D$ measures how far the fitted model is from the best possible fit. This is what `deviance()` returns for `glm` objects, and what is shown as null deviance (D of the intercept-only model) and residual deviance (D of the fitted model) in `summary()` and in the `anova()` tables of GLMs. For a normal linear model, $D$ is the residual sum of squares (RSS; divided by $\sigma^2$ for the scaled deviance), which is why the deviance plays the role of the sum of squares in GLMs (see @sec-anova-example for the sums of squares in ANOVA). For 0/1 binomial data, $\log L(\text{saturated}) = 0$, and thus $D = -2 \log L$.
2.  **Deviance as** $-2 \log L$: in many mixed-model contexts, $-2 \log L(\text{fitted})$ is called the deviance (older versions of `lme4` did this in their `anova()` tables, and `deviance()` for `lmer` fits still returns it; newer `lme4` versions and `glmmTMB` print it as `-2*log(L)`). It is the same as $D$ without the term $2 \log L(\text{saturated})$. AIC is built on this quantity, $\mathrm{AIC} = -2 \log L + 2k$.

The two definitions differ by $2 \log L(\text{saturated})$, which is the same for all models fitted to the same data. Therefore, *differences* between models agree for both definitions as long as the dispersion is fixed (e.g. Poisson, binomial), and likelihood ratio tests and AIC comparisons give the same results. The *absolute values* are different, and numbers calculated with the two definitions must not be compared. For normal linear models, differences in RSS and differences in $-2 \log L$ are not identical, because the variance is estimated: at the maximum likelihood estimate, $-2 \log L = n \log(\mathrm{RSS}/n) + n (1 + \log 2\pi)$.
:::

::: callout-note
**Example:** we can calculate the deviance by hand, using a saturated model with one parameter per observation.

Deviance of M~1~

```{r}
fit1 = glm(feeding ~ attractiveness, data = birdfeeding, family = "poisson")
summary(fit1)$deviance
fitSat = glm(feeding ~ as.factor(1:nrow(birdfeeding)), data = birdfeeding, family = "poisson")
2*(logLik(fitSat) - logLik(fit1))
```

Deviance of the null model (null model is for example needed to calculate the pseudo-R^2^ ):

```{r}
summary(fit1)$null.deviance
fitNull = glm(feeding ~ 1, data = birdfeeding, family = "poisson")
2*(logLik(fitSat) - logLik(fitNull))
```

**Calculation of Pseudo-R^2^** **with deviance or logL**

Common pseudo-R^2^ such as McFadden or Nagelkerke use the logL instead of the deviance, whereas the deviance-based pseudo-R^2^ (1 - D~res~/D~null~, the "proportion of deviance explained") uses the deviance. However, R^2^ calculated based on deviance or logL differs considerably, as the former is calculated in reference to the maximal achievable fit (saturated model) while the latter just compares the improvement of fit compared to the null model:

```{r}
# Based on logL
McFadden = 1-(logLik(fit1))/(logLik(fitNull))
print(McFadden)

# Based on deviance
R2_dev = 1- (logLik(fitSat) - logLik(fit1)) / (logLik(fitSat) - logLik(fitNull))
print(R2_dev)
```
:::

If we want to calculate model predictions, we have to transform to the response scale. Here we have a log link, i.e. we have to transform with exp(linear response).

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk17, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
exp(coef(fit)[1] + 3 * coef(fit)[2])
```

Alternatively (and preferably), you can use the predict() function with `type = "response"`

```{r}
dat = data.frame(attractiveness = 3)
predict(fit, newdata = dat) # linear predictor
predict(fit, newdata = dat, type = "response") # response scale
```

Because of the log link, effects are multiplicative: `exp(coef(fit))` shows that each unit of attractiveness multiplies the expected number of feedings by about 1.16 (a rate ratio, see @tbl-summary-link for the interpretation of coefficients under the common link functions).

Effect plots work as before (see @sec-lm-visualization). Note that the effects package always transforms the y axis according to the link, so we have log scaling on the y axis, and the effect lines remain straight

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(effects)
plot(allEffects(fit))
```

#### Notes on the Poisson regression {#sec-glm-poisson-note}

**Poisson vs. log transformed count data:** For count data, even if the distribution is switched, the log link is nearly always the appropriate link function. Before GLMs were widely available, it was common to fit an lm to log-transformed counts (log(y + 1) if there are zeros). This is similar to, but not the same as, a Poisson GLM with log link: the lm assumes a constant variance on the log scale, the Poisson GLM a variance equal to the mean (see also @sec-glm-gamma).

**Log offset:** If there is a variable that controls the number of counts (e.g. time, area), this variable is usually added as an offset in the following form

```{r, eval = F}
fit = glm(y ~ x + offset(log(area)), family = "poisson")
```

To see why this is useful, consider that with the log link

$$y  = exp(a_0 + a_1 \cdot x + log(area) )$$

and then rewriting

$$y  = exp(a_0 + a_1 \cdot x) \dot exp(log(area)) $$

i.e. this makes the expected counts proportional to area, or whatever variable is added as a log offset.

**Interactions:** As for all GLMs with nonlinear link functions, interpretation of the interactions is more complicated. See the section on interactions in GLMs (@sec-glm-interaction) for notes on this.

### 0/1 or k/n data - logistic regression {#sec-glm-logistic}

The standard model to fit binomial (0/1 or k/n) data is the logistic regression, which combines the binomial distribution with a logit link function. To get to know this model, let's have a look at the titanic data set in EcoData:

```{r}
library(EcoData)
#str(titanic)
#mosaicplot( ~ survived + sex + pclass, data = titanic)
titanic$pclass = as.factor(titanic$pclass)
```

We want to analyze how survival in the titanic accident depended on other predictors. We could fit an lm, but the residual checks make it very evident that the data with a 0/1 response don't fit to the assumption of an lm:

```{r}
fit = lm(survived ~ sex * age, data = titanic)
summary(fit)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)
```

Thus, let's move to the logistic regression, which assumes a 0/1 response + logit link. In principle, this distribution is called Bernoulli, but in R both 0/1 and k/n are called "binomial", as Bernoulli is the special case of binomial where n = 1.

```{r}
m1 = glm(survived ~ sex*age, family = "binomial", data = titanic)
summary(m1)
```

::: callout-note
The syntax here is for 0/1 data. If you have k/n data, you can either specify the response as cbind(k, n-k), or you can fit the glm with `I(k/n) ~ x, weights = n` (and `family = binomial`)
:::

The coefficients are now on the logit scale (log odds, where odds = p/(1-p)); `exp(coef(m1))` gives odds ratios (see @tbl-summary-link). To transform to predictions, we have to use the inverse logit, which is in R:

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk5, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
cf = coef(m1)
plogis(cf[1] + cf[3] * 20)  # Women, age 20.
plogis(cf[1] + cf[2] + 20 * (cf[3] + cf[4])) # Men, age 20
```

Alternatively, we can again use the predict function

```{r}
newDat = data.frame(sex = as.factor(c("female", "male")), age = c(20,20))
predict(m1, newdata = newDat) # Linear predictor.
predict(m1, newdata = newDat, type = "response")  # Response scale.
```

Finally, the effect plots - note again the scaling of the y axis, which is now logit.

```{r}
library(effects)
plot(allEffects(m1))
```

If you do an ANOVA on a glm, you should take care that you perform a Chisq and not an F-test. You notice that you have the right one if the ANOVA doesn't supply SumSq statistics, but deviance. In the anova function, we have to set this by hand

```{r}
anova(m1, test = "Chisq")
```

`anova()` on a single model gives sequential (type I) tests, and only for some model classes (e.g. `lm`, `glm`, `gls`; for `glmer` it gives no p-values, for `glmmTMB` no such method exists). The function car::Anova works for most model classes and uses a ChiSq test automatically (for glm this is a likelihood-ratio test; for glmer/glmmTMB, `car::Anova` computes Wald chi-squared tests, which are approximate). It gives type II tests by default (type III with `type = "III"`, which needs sum-to-zero contrasts, @cau-glm-before); as you probably want one of these anyway, prefer it.

```{r, message=FALSE}
car::Anova(m1)
```

::: {#cau-glm-before .callout-caution}
#### Before testing a GLM

- **Check dispersion first.** For Poisson and k/n binomial models, overdispersion (see the section on dispersion problems, @sec-glm-dispersion) makes all p-values of `car::Anova()` and `summary()` too small. It is not unusual that a seemingly highly significant effect disappears once the dispersion is accounted for. Refit with a negative binomial or beta-binomial family (@sec-glm-dispersion); quasi-families are discouraged (no residual checks, no AIC), and if you use one anyway, test with `car::Anova(m, test.statistic = "F")`.
- **Coding and centering.** The rules for type II vs. III, sum-to-zero contrasts and centering from the chapter on ANOVA (@sec-anova-contrast) also apply to GLMs; averages are taken on the link scale.
- **Reporting on the response scale.** `emmeans(m, ~ x, type = "response")` back-transforms the means, and `pairs()` then gives ratios (log link) or odds ratios (logit link); for differences and data-averaged effects on the response scale, see @sec-glm-effects.
:::

For GLMMs, `car::Anova()` gives Wald tests that treat the estimated random-effect variances as exact and ignore the df problem of mixed models (@sec-re-df), so with few groups the p-values are too small; for alternatives, see @tbl-glm-glmmtest.

#### Notes on the logistic regression {#sec-glm-logistic-note}

**Offset:** for 0/1 data with different exposure times t, as in survival analysis, a binomial GLM with cloglog link and `offset(log(t))` models a constant hazard exactly (P(event) = 1 - exp(-lambda t)). The logit link has no such interpretation.

**Interactions:** As for all GLMs with nonlinear link functions, interpretation of the interactions is more complicated. See the section on interactions in GLMs (@sec-glm-interaction) for notes on this.

**Overdispersion:** 0/1 binomial responses cannot be overdispersed, but k/n responses can be. However, 0/1 responses can show overdispersion if grouped to k/n. Note the section on residual checks (@sec-glm-residual), in particular the dispersion problems (@sec-glm-dispersion), as well as comments on testing binomial GLMs in the\
[DHARMa vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DHARMa/vignettes/DHARMa.html#binomial-data).

**More than two categories:** if the response is one of several unordered categories (e.g. land-use type, type of food chosen), the logistic regression generalizes to the multinomial logistic regression (`nnet::multinom`; with random effects, `brms` with family `categorical`). It estimates one set of coefficients for each category, as log odds ratios relative to a reference category. The response can be one category per observation or the counts per category for each unit (e.g. number of food items of each type). If the categories are ordered (e.g. damage classes, Likert scales), use a cumulative link model (`ordinal::clm`, or `clmm` with random effects), which assumes that each predictor has the same effect on all thresholds between categories (check with `ordinal::nominal_test()`). If several categories can apply at the same time, the response is not multinomial, but several binary responses (see the multivariate GLMs, @sec-corr-multivar). Variants exist for choices with alternative-specific predictors (`mlogit`) and for matched case-control designs (`survival::clogit`).

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise — Elk data

Consider the following dataset

```{r}
library(EcoData)
str(elk)
```

on habitat use of Elks in Canada. Measured is the presence of Elks (0/1), and a number of other predictors that are described in the help (`?elk`). As we have 0/1 data, we fit a binomial GLM (logistic regression).

Perform either:

a)  A predictive analysis, i.e. a model to predict where Elks can be found.
b)  A causal analysis, trying to understand the effect of roads on Elk presence. For this:
    1.  Check the help of the data (`?elk`) and consider which variables you should adjust for in a multiple GLM, based on the ideas explained in the chapter on causal analysis (@sec-causal).
    2.  After specifying the multiple regression, check the residuals of your model to make sure it's properly specified, including residual plots against all predictors. If you find misfits, consider the use of splines (@sec-lm-gam), which can be specified by replacing the glm with the `mgcv::gam` function.
    3.  Bonus: read up on checking residuals of logistic regressions in the [DHARMa vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DHARMa/vignettes/DHARMa.html#binomial-data).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

A. Predictive analysis

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(MASS)
fit <- glm(presence ~ dist_roads  + dem + ruggedness, data = elk, family = "binomial")
predictive_model = MASS::stepAIC(fit, direction = "both")
summary(predictive_model)

```

B. Causal analysis

The predictive model has actually dropped the variable of interest (distance to roads) which shows the risks of tools that select for the best predictive model such as AIC selection (see @sec-select-causality): Collinear variables that we need to adjust our effects, are often dropped.

For the causal model, we really need to think about the causal relationships between the variables:

We are interested in the effect of dist_roads on presence:

```{r}
summary(glm(presence ~ dist_roads, data = elk, family = "binomial"))
```

The effect of dist_roads is positive: the probability of finding elk increases with the distance to roads, i.e. there are fewer elk close to roads. This would fit the idea that elk avoid roads, but we can't interpret this causally yet, because roads are not placed randomly in the landscape.

Altitude (dem) and the ruggedness probably affect both variables, presence and dist_roads (roads are mostly built in low and flat terrain), and thus they should be considered as confounders:

```{r}
fit = glm(presence ~ dist_roads+ dem + ruggedness, data = elk, family = "binomial")
summary(fit)
```

After adjusting for altitude and ruggedness, the effect of dist_roads is no longer positive, but close to zero and n.s. Thus, the crude effect was mainly caused by the confounders: elk occur in terrain where there are fewer roads.

Let's check the residuals:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(DHARMa)
res <- simulateResiduals(fit)
plot(res, quantreg = TRUE) # quantreg adds the quantile lines (off by default for n > 2000)
plotResiduals(res, form = elk$dem, quantreg = TRUE)
plotResiduals(res, form = elk$ruggedness, quantreg = TRUE)
```

The functional forms of our confounders are not perfect.

Since we are not really interested in them, we model the confounders flexibly with a GAM, as in the section on statistical control (@sec-causal-adjustment). Our main predictor dist_roads is still modeled as a linear effect.

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(mgcv)
fit2 <- gam(presence ~ dist_roads + s(dem) + s(ruggedness), data = elk, family = "binomial")
summary(fit2)
```

Let's take another look at the residual plots, in particular for the confounders.

```{r, message=FALSE}
res <- simulateResiduals(fit2)
plot(res, quantreg = TRUE) # with quantile lines
plotResiduals(res, form = elk$dem, quantreg = TRUE)
plotResiduals(res, form = elk$ruggedness, quantreg = TRUE)
```

Now, the quantile plots show no obvious misfit. With the confounders modeled flexibly, the effect of dist_roads is negative and significant: at the same altitude and ruggedness, elk are found slightly closer to roads. The crude effect has thus even changed its sign once the confounders were properly accounted for. Note that we did not choose the final model because the sign of the effect matched our expectations (it doesn't), but because it includes the confounders and passes the residual checks. Judging a model by whether its estimates look plausible is a common, but dangerous, way to fool yourself.
:::

### Continuous positive response - Gamma regression {#sec-glm-gamma}

The Gamma regression is the natural choice for a **strictly positive, continuous, right-skewed** response whose variance grows with the mean (e.g. concentrations, waiting times, biomass, body sizes). A common alternative is to log-transform and fit an `lm` (as we do first below), but the two are not equivalent: the log-`lm` assumes constant variance *on the log scale* and, if you back-transform predictions, incurs a retransformation bias, whereas the Gamma GLM models the mean on the original scale with a variance that scales as $\text{Var}(y) \propto \mu^2$. With a log link (which we set explicitly below, because R's default for `Gamma()` is the inverse link, see the box below), coefficients are interpreted multiplicatively - `exp(coef)` is the factor by which the mean changes per unit of the predictor, as in the Poisson regression.

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(faraway)
```

```{r}
fit <- lm(log(resist) ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = wafer)
summary(fit)

library(DHARMa)
simulateResiduals(fit, plot = T)
```

Alternative: Gamma regression

```{r}
fit <- glm(formula = resist ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4,
           family  = Gamma(link = "log"),
           data    = wafer)
summary(fit)
```

::: callout-note
For Gamma regression, different link functions are used. The canonical link, which is also the default in R, is the inverse link 1/x. However, also log and identity link are commonly used.
:::

### Continuous proportions: beta regression and alternatives {#sec-glm-beta}

We already covered discrete proportions (k successes out of n trials), which can be modeled with a logistic regression (@sec-glm-logistic). Many proportions, however, are continuous: a fraction of an area, a concentration, a share of time spent in an activity. For these, there is no number of trials, so the binomial does not apply.

Before choosing a model, check how the proportion was measured:

- **Counts out of a known total** (e.g. germinated seeds out of seeds sown) are k/n data: use a binomial GLM, or a beta-binomial (`family = betabinomial` in glmmTMB) if they are overdispersed [@douma2019beta].
- **Ordered classes** (e.g. 0-5%, 5-25%, 25-50%, ...) are ordinal data (see the notes on the logistic regression, @sec-glm-logistic-note). Analyzing class midpoints as if they were measured values ignores how coarse the classes are.
- **Continuous values** are the topic of this section.

For continuous proportions, there are several reasonable options. The most common are presented in the following table:

| Model | R | Can handle 0/1 | Use when |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| transformation + `lm` | `qlogis(y)` | only after adding a constant | quick analysis with few 0/1 [@warton2011arcsine]; check sensitivity to the constant |
| beta regression | `beta_family()` | only after squeezing into (0, 1); with many 0/1, ordered or hurdle beta are better | all values strictly between 0 and 1 |
| ordered beta | `ordbeta()` | yes | 0 and 1 are the ends of the same scale (e.g. values below a detection limit) |
| hurdle beta | `beta_family()` + `ziformula`; with 1s: `brms` | 0 only (`ziformula`); 0 and 1: `brms` (`zero_one_inflated_beta`) | the zeros arise from a different process than the other values |

The logit transform is a quick fix. The standard distribution for continuous proportions, however, is the beta distribution. It is bounded between 0 and 1 and has two parameters: the mean and the precision $\phi$. A large $\phi$ means that values scatter little around the mean. glmmTMB prints $\phi$ as "Dispersion parameter", which is confusing: for the beta, a large value means a narrow distribution. Like the binomial, the beta is naturally heteroskedastic: its variance is largest for a mean of 0.5 and shrinks towards 0 and 1. As in the logistic regression, the mean is modeled with a logit link, so coefficients are on the logit scale.

::: callout-tip
#### Example: nitrogen in leaves

We use the `elemental` data from EcoData (`?elemental`), which contain the nitrogen content of leaves as a proportion (`N_dec`; `N_arc` is its arcsine square root transformation, included in the data). There are no zeros or ones, so a standard beta regression applies.

The arcsine transformation was long the standard approach for proportions, but @warton2011arcsine showed that it should be avoided; we fit it here only for comparison:

```{r}
abba <- elemental[elemental$Species == "ABBA", ]
m1 <- lm(N_arc ~ Year + Site, data = abba)
summary(m1)
```

Now a beta regression:

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)
m2 <- glmmTMB(N_dec ~ Year + Site, family = beta_family, data = abba)
summary(m2)
plot(simulateResiduals(m2))
```

Both models find an increase of leaf nitrogen over the years. The beta regression models the bounded response directly, and its residuals show no problems.
:::

**Dealing with 0/1 observations:** The beta distribution is defined only strictly between 0 and 1, so exact zeros or ones need an extension. The **hurdle beta** (in glmmTMB: zero-inflated beta) works like zero-inflation for counts (@sec-glm-zero-inflation), but because a beta never produces an exact 0, the zero part is a separate logistic model for the zeros. A predictor can therefore affect whether a value is zero and how large it is otherwise in different ways [@douma2019beta]. The **ordered beta** [@kubinec2023ordered] uses a single linear predictor plus two thresholds on the logit scale that decide when a value is exactly 0 or 1. It assumes that a predictor that raises the mean of the continuous part also lowers the probability of a 0, and it needs fewer parameters when there are several predictors. The ordered beta was introduced only in 2022, so applied studies more often use zero/one-inflated or hurdle models. Other options are to squeeze the data into (0, 1) before a beta regression [@smithson2006better], a quasibinomial GLM (no likelihood, so no AIC and no DHARMa residuals), or quantile regression (@sec-disp-quantile). The beta models in glmmTMB (beta, ordered beta, hurdle beta) can include random effects, and their precision can depend on predictors (`dispformula`, @sec-disp-model). An example with zeros follows in the case study on plant cover (@sec-glm-cover).

#### Several proportions from the same unit {#sec-glm-shares}

If you analyze several proportions measured on the same unit (e.g. cover of several plant species in a plot, the time an animal spends on different activities, land-use shares of a region), their residuals are usually correlated, for example because they share unmeasured conditions of that unit. Separate models are fine for questions about one response at a time, but comparisons or sums across responses need a joint model (@sec-corr-multivar). If the proportions are shares of a whole that sum to exactly 1 (e.g. diet composition), Dirichlet regression respects this constraint (e.g. `brms` family `dirichlet`). The Dirichlet does not allow exact zeros: zeros must be squeezed into (0, 1) or modeled with a zero-augmented Dirichlet; if the shares come from counts (e.g. number of food items), use a multinomial model instead [@douma2019beta].

## Residuals and their solutions in GLMs {#sec-glm-residual}

::: {#residual-and-their-solutions-in-glms}
:::

First of all: everything we said about residual checks for LMs (@sec-lm-residual) and about model selection (@sec-select) also applies for GLMs, with only very few additions, so you should check your model in principle as before. However, there are a few tweaks you have to be aware of.

Let's look again at the titanic example

```{r}
m1 = glm(survived ~ sex*age, family = "binomial", data = titanic)
```

How can we check the residuals of this model? The standard residual plots still run (Nerds: check `class(m1)`), but they look horrible, because they check for normally distributed residuals, whereas ours should be binomial:

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk10, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(m1)
```

### DHARMa residual plots for GL(M)Ms {#sec-glm-dharma}

The DHARMa residuals solve this problem: they are simulated from the fitted model, so they work for any family and are read as for the linear model (@sec-lm-residual-dharma).

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk12, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
library(DHARMa)
res = simulateResiduals(m1)
```

Standard plot:

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk13, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
plot(res)
```

The Q-Q plot (left) follows the 1-1 line and the residuals vs. predicted plot (right) shows no pattern, so these two plots show no problem. The residuals against the predictors also show no particular problem:

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk14, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotResiduals(res, form = model.frame(m1)$age)
plotResiduals(res, form = model.frame(m1)$sex)
```

However, residuals against the missing predictor pclass show a clear problem:

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk15, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dataUsed = as.numeric(rownames(model.frame(m1)))
plotResiduals(res, form = titanic$pclass[dataUsed])
```

Thus, I should add passenger class to the model

```{r}
m2 = glm(survived ~ sex*age + pclass, family = "binomial", data = titanic)
summary(m2)

res2 = simulateResiduals(m2)
plotResiduals(res2, form = model.frame(m2)$pclass)
```

Now, residuals look fine. Of course, if your model gets more complicated, you may want to do additional checks, for example for the distribution of random effects etc.

### Dispersion problems in GLMs {#sec-glm-dispersion}

One thing that is different between GLMs and LM is that GLMs can display overall dispersion problems. The most common GLMs to show overdispersion are the Poisson and the binomial with k/n data (0/1 data cannot be overdispersed).

The reason is that simple GLM distributions such as the Poisson or the Binomial (for k/n data) do not have a parameter for adjusting the spread of the observed data around the regression line (dispersion), but their variance is a fixed function of the mean.

There are good reasons for why this is the case (Poisson and Binomial describe particular processes, e.g. coin flip, for which the variance is a fixed function of the mean), but the fact is that when applying these GLMs on real data, we often find overdispersion (more dispersion than expected), and more rarely, underdispersion (less dispersion than expected).

To remove the assumptions of a fixed dispersion, there are three options, of which I usually prefer the third one:

1.  **Quasi-distributions**, which are available in glm. Those add a term to the likelihood that corrects the p-values for the dispersion, but they are not distributions, so there are no residual checks and no AIC. Therefore discouraged.
2.  **Observation-level random effect (OLRE)** - Add a separate random effect per observation. This effectively creates a normal random variate at the level of the linear predictor, increases variance on the responses.
3.  A **GLM distribution with variable dispersion**, for Poisson usually the negative binomial, for k/n binomial data the beta-binomial (`family = betabinomial` in glmmTMB).

The reason why I prefer the 3rd option is that it allows better residual checks and to model the dispersion as a function of the predictors (see @sec-disp-glmm). OLRE is also a valid solution.

::: callout-note
Overdispersion is often created by model misfit. Thus, before moving to a variable dispersion GLM, you should check for / correct model misfit.
:::

#### Recognizing overdispersion {#sec-glm-overdispersion-detect}

To understand how to recognize overdispersion, let's look at an example. We'll use the Salamanders dataset from the package glmmTMB, staring with a simple Poisson glm:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(glmmTMB)
library(lme4)
library(DHARMa)

m1 = glm(count ~ spp + mined, family = poisson, data = Salamanders)
```

Overdispersion will be automatically highlighted in the standard DHARMa plots

```{r, message=FALSE}
res = simulateResiduals(m1, plot = T)
```

You see the dispersion problem by:

- Dispersion test in the left plot significant

- QQ plot S-shaped

- Quantile lines in the right plots outside their expected quantiles

You can get a more detailed output with the testDispersion function, which also displays the direction of the dispersion problem (over or underdispersion)

```{r}
testDispersion(res)
```

OK, often the dispersion problem is caused by structural problems. Let's add a random effect for site, which makes sense. We can do so using the function lme4::glmer, which adds the same extensions to glm as lmer adds to lm. This means we can use the usual random effect syntax from @sec-re-intercept.

```{r}
m2 = glmer(count ~ spp + mined + (1|site), 
           family = poisson, data = Salamanders)
```

Testing the residuals

```{r, message=FALSE}
res = simulateResiduals(m2, plot = T)
```

shows that there is still some overdispersion. Actually, what the plots also show is heteroskedasticity, and we should probably deal with that as well, but we will only learn how in the next chapter on dispersion models (@sec-disp). For now, let's switch to a negative binomial model. This could be fit with lme4, but it is more convenient to use the package glmmTMB, which has the same syntax as lme4, but more advanced options.

```{r}
m3 = glmmTMB(count ~ spp + mined + (1|site), family = nbinom2, data = Salamanders)
res = simulateResiduals(m3, plot = T)
```

Now, the test is fine. The negative binomial is a Poisson distribution with a gamma-distributed rate. `glmmTMB` offers two parameterizations: `nbinom2` (variance $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$, quadratic in the mean, the usual starting point) and `nbinom1` (variance $\mu (1 + \alpha)$, linear in the mean); compare both by AIC if in doubt.

### Zero-inflation {#sec-glm-zero-inflation}

Another common problem in count data (Poisson / negative binomial), but also other GLMs (e.g. binomial, beta) is that the observed data has more zeros than expected by the fitted distribution. For the beta, 1-inflation, and for the k/n binomial, n-inflation is also common, and tested for / addressed in the same way.

To deal with this **zero-inflation**, one usually adds an additional model component that controls how many zeros are produced. The default way to do this is assuming two separate processes which act after one another:

1.  First, we have the normal GLM, predicting what values we would expect
2.  On top of that, we have a logistic regression, which decides whether the GLM prediction or a zero should be observed

Note that the result of 1 can also be zero, so there are two explanations for a zero in the data. Zero-inflated GLMMs can, for example, be fit with glmmTMB, using the ziformula argument.

#### Recognizing zero-inflation {#sec-glm-zero-inflation-detect}

::: callout-caution
The fact that you have a lot of zeros in your data does not indicate zero-inflation. Zero-inflation is with respect to the fitted model. You can only check for zero-inflation after fitting a model.
:::

Let's look at our last model - DHARMa has a special function to check for zero-inflation

```{r chunk_chapter5_chunk22, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testZeroInflation(res)
```

This shows no sign of zero-inflation. There are, however, two problems with this test:

1.  For mixed models, the test is less powerful with unconditional residuals, because the re-simulated random effects add variation (@tip-re-predtype). This happens if you set `simulateREs = "unconditional"`, or if DHARMa cannot simulate conditionally for the model's covariance structure and falls back to unconditional simulations (it then says so in a message).
2.  When there is really zero-inflation, variable dispersion models such as the negative Binomial often simply increase the dispersion to account for the zeros, leading to no apparent zero-inflation in the residuals, but rather underdispersion.

Thus, for zero-inflation, model selection, or simply fitting a ZIP model is often more reliable than residual checks. Compare the models with and without `ziformula` via AIC or likelihood ratio test. Do not use the p-value of the zero-inflation intercept for this, as it tests a zero-inflation probability of 0.5, not the absence of zero-inflation.

```{r}
m4 = glmmTMB(count ~ spp + mined + (1|site), family = nbinom2, ziformula = ~1,  data = Salamanders)
summary(m4)
```

In this case, we have no evidence for zero-inflation (AIC 1674.4 with vs. 1672.4 without zero-inflation, i.e. the simpler model is preferred; the estimated zero-inflation intercept of about -16 on the logit scale, i.e. a probability of about 0, with a huge standard error is a boundary estimate). To see an example where you can find zero-inflation, see the owls exercise (@cau-glm-owls).

## Interpreting effects and interactions in GLMs {#sec-glm-interaction}

::: {#interpreting-interactions-in-glms}
:::

A significant problem with interpreting GLMs is the interpretation of effects, in particular of interactions. To see the problem, let's simulate survival data in which the treatment and the concentration of a substance act additively on the probability scale: the treatment raises survival from 30% to 80%, and the concentration adds up to 15% in both groups. We might think that there is no interaction, but a logistic regression finds a clearly positive interaction coefficient (z ≈ 5):

```{r}
library(effects)
set.seed(1)
n = 20000
trt = as.factor(sample(c("ctrl", "trt"), n, replace = TRUE))
concentration = runif(n)
response = 0.3 + 0.5 * (as.numeric(trt) - 1) + 0.15 * concentration
survival = rbinom(n, 1, prob = response)
dat = data.frame(trt = trt, concentration = concentration, survival = survival)

m2 = glm(survival ~ trt * concentration, data = dat, family = "binomial")
summary(m2)
plot(allEffects(m2))
```

The reason is the link function: a coefficient is a constant change on the logit scale, and the same change on the logit scale translates into different changes of the probability, depending on where we start. If we plot the `plogis()` function, this becomes obvious: at a baseline near 0.4 (control), one unit on the logit scale changes the probability by a lot, at a baseline near 0.9 (treatment) by much less.

```{r, echo= F}
curve(plogis, -6, 6, xlab = "linear predictor", ylab = "probability")
abline(v = 0)
abline(v = 1, lty = 2)
abline(v = 3, col = "red")
abline(v = 4, col = "red", lty =2)
```

Turned around: for the same effect of concentration on the probability scale in both groups, the model needs an interaction on the logit scale. The effect plots show this as well, but note that they scale the y axis according to the link, so the lines look straight and the slopes look different. Whether a "real" interaction is one on the link scale or one on the response scale is a biological decision: one could argue that a change of 15% in survival means something different at 30% than at 80% survival. Decide this from your question before looking at the results; a link-scale interaction can appear or disappear depending on the scale, and choosing the scale after seeing which one gives the result you like is a forking path (@sec-select-problems).

::: callout-note
If effect directions change in sign, they will do so under any link function (as they are always monotone), so changes in effect direction are robust to this problem.
:::

### Ways to report an effect {#sec-glm-effects}

The effect of a predictor on the response scale depends on all other predictors. As in the linear model (@sec-lm-nonlinear-effect; effects plots to look at the model, `emmeans` for the numbers), you can report the curve or predictions at chosen values, slopes or differences at chosen values, and the data-averaged effect; in a GLM, a fourth option appears, the ratio, which is constant on the link scale. In a linear model without interactions or curvature, the slope at the mean equals the data-averaged slope; in a GLM it does not.

| What | Scale | Averaged over | Call |
|----|----|----|----|
| Curve or predictions at chosen values | response | nothing | effects plots; `emmeans(m, ~ trt, at = list(...), type = "response")` |
| Slopes or differences at chosen values | response | nothing | `emtrends(m, ~ trt, var = "x", regrid = "response")`; `pairs(regrid(emmeans(...)))` |
| Data-averaged effect: the difference (factor) or slope (numeric predictor) on the response scale, averaged over all observations | response | the observed data | factors: `emmeans(m, ~ trt, counterfactuals = "trt", type = "response")`; slopes: finite differences |
| Ratio: rate ratio (log link), odds ratio (logit link) | link scale, back-transformed | nothing (constant without interactions; with interactions it depends on the other predictors) | `exp(coef(m))`; `pairs(emmeans(m, ~ trt, type = "response"))` |

**Ratios.** For our model, the odds ratio of the treatment is

```{r}
library(emmeans)
pairs(emmeans(m2, ~ trt, type = "response"), reverse = TRUE)
```

i.e. the odds of survival are about 12 times higher under treatment, evaluated at the mean concentration (`emmeans` may warn that the result can be misleading because of the interaction: the odds ratio changes with the concentration). Ratios arise because a logit-link model is additive in log-odds, and adding on a log scale means multiplying: a coefficient becomes a factor on the odds (with a log link, a factor on the expected count, the rate ratio). Ratios are compact and constant on the link scale, which is why they are the standard way to report GLM coefficients (@tbl-summary-link), but they are hard to read: an odds ratio is not a risk ratio, and an odds ratio of 12 does not tell you whether survival went from 1% to 11% or from 30% to 84%.

**Predictions on the response scale** at chosen values of the other predictors answer this directly:

```{r}
emmeans(m2, ~ trt | concentration, at = list(concentration = c(0.2, 0.8)), type = "response")
```

The confidence intervals are back-transformed from the logit scale and therefore asymmetric and bounded by 0 and 1.

**The data-averaged effect** answers the question "by how much did the treatment change survival on average in this sample". With `counterfactuals`, `emmeans` predicts every observation once as control and once as treated (with its own concentration), averages the predictions on the probability scale and compares them:

```{r}
emmC = emmeans(m2, ~ trt, counterfactuals = "trt", type = "response")
emmC
confint(contrast(emmC, "revpairwise"))
```

The treatment raised survival by 0.49 on average (the true value is 0.50). This quantity is the G-computation (also called standardization) estimate of an average causal effect (@sec-causal), it refers to the covariate distribution of this sample, its standard error assumes that the model is right (check the residuals first, @sec-glm-residual), and the predictor must be a factor (a 0/1 predictor is treated as numeric). The output label `actual_trt` refers to the observed treatment, over which the predictions are averaged.

For a numeric predictor, the data-averaged slope on the probability scale follows from finite differences as in @sec-lm-nonlinear-effect, here per treatment group:

```{r}
h = 0.01
d = (predict(m2, transform(dat, concentration = concentration + h), type = "response") -
     predict(m2, transform(dat, concentration = concentration - h), type = "response")) / (2 * h)
tapply(d, dat$trt, mean)
```

`emtrends()` with `regrid = "response"` gives instead the slope of the probability at the mean of the other predictors (shown in the next subsection); in our example, the two differ by less than 0.01. The `marginaleffects` package [@arelbundock2024interpret] computes such average effects and slopes directly for many model classes; in this book, we stay with `emmeans`.

**Which one to report?** Always show the curve or the predictions, as for linear models; add one summary number. In a designed experiment with few covariates, a ratio or the difference at reference values is fine; for observational data, interactions or several covariates, the data-averaged effect is usually the most useful single number. For GLMMs, `counterfactuals` gives the data-averaged effect for a typical group, not a marginal one (@sec-glm-marginal). In all cases, say which scale and which averaging you used, e.g. "treatment increased survival by 0.49 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.50), averaged over the observed concentrations (data-averaged effect)", or "the odds of survival were 12 times higher under treatment (95% CI 11 to 13) at the mean concentration".

### Interactions on the response scale {#sec-glm-interaction-response}

With these tools, we can now judge the interaction of our example on the scale we decided on. On the logit scale, the slopes of concentration clearly differ between the groups:

```{r}
emtrends(m2, ~ trt, var = "concentration")
```

On the probability scale, they do not:

```{r}
emtrends(m2, ~ trt, var = "concentration", regrid = "response")
pairs(emtrends(m2, ~ trt, var = "concentration", regrid = "response"))
```

So the rule is: a significant interaction on the link scale says nothing about whether the effects are additive on the response scale, and vice versa. Judge an interaction by differences of slopes or of effects on the scale that you decided on; for two factors, `contrast(regrid(emmeans(m, ~ A * B)), interaction = "pairwise")` gives the difference of differences on the response scale. Note also that main effects and interactions can change if you change the link function, and that default links are not always natural from a biological viewpoint.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise — Effects on the count scale

The `warpbreaks` data set (base R) contains the number of breaks in yarn for two types of wool (A, B) and three levels of tension (L, M, H). Fit `glm(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = warpbreaks, family = poisson)` and report the effect of tension (a) as rate ratios and (b) as data-averaged differences in the number of breaks. Then judge whether wool and tension interact on the count scale, and compare with the interaction on the link scale.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

```{r}
m = glm(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = warpbreaks, family = poisson)
# (a) rate ratios, averaged over wool on the link scale
pairs(emmeans(m, ~ tension, type = "response"), reverse = TRUE)
# (b) data-averaged differences in breaks
emmT = emmeans(m, ~ tension, counterfactuals = "tension", type = "response")
confint(contrast(emmT, "revpairwise"))
# interaction on the count scale (difference of differences) and on the link scale (ratio of ratios)
contrast(regrid(emmeans(m, ~ tension * wool)), interaction = "pairwise")
contrast(emmeans(m, ~ tension * wool), interaction = "pairwise", type = "response")
# simple effects of tension within each wool type, on the count scale
contrast(regrid(emmeans(m, ~ tension | wool)), "revpairwise")
```

Medium and high tension reduce breaks by 26% and 39% relative to low tension (rate ratios 0.74 and 0.61), i.e. by 10 and 15 breaks on average. An interaction is present on both scales (L-M: ratio of ratios 1.9, difference of differences 21 breaks; the interaction contrasts are not adjusted for multiple testing): for wool A, both higher tensions reduce breaks by about 20, for wool B only high tension has an effect (-9 breaks). Here the conclusion does not depend on the scale, but the numbers do: on the link scale, the L-H contrast does not differ between the wool types (ratio of ratios 1.2, p = 0.15), on the count scale it does (difference of differences 10.6 breaks, p = 0.003), because the same ratio means more breaks at the higher counts of wool A. The scale can thus change whether an interaction contrast is significant, which is why the scale should be decided beforehand.
:::

## New considerations for GLMMs {#sec-glm-glmm}

::: {#new-considerations-for-glmms}
:::

As we saw, in principle, random effects can be added to GLMs very much in the same way as before (@sec-re). Note, however, that there is a conceptual difference:

1.  In an LMM, we had y = f(x) + RE + residual, where both RE and residual error were normal distributions

2.  In a GLMM, we have $y \sim dist[link^{-1}(f(x) + RE)]$, so the normally distributed RE goes through the inverse link into the response distribution

This has a number of consequences that may be unexpected if you don't think about it.

### Unconditional vs. marginal predictions {#sec-glm-marginal}

A consequence of the inverse link is that, with a nonlinear link function, unconditional predictions (fixed effects only) differ from marginal predictions (averaged over the random effects) and thus from the mean of your data; the three kinds of predictions are defined in @tip-re-predterms. To understand this, imagine we have a logistic regression, and our fixed effects predict a mean of 1. Then the unconditional prediction at the response scale

```{r}
plogis(1)
```

Now, let's try to see what the average (marginal) prediction over all random effects is. We simulate random intercepts from a normal distribution with sd = 1 (1e5 draws). In this case, there will be additional variation around the random intercept.

```{r}
mean(plogis(1 + rnorm(1e5, sd = 1)))
```

The value (about 0.70) is lower than the unconditional prediction (0.73), and this value is also what you would approximately get if you take the mean of your data.

Whether this is a problem or not is a matter of perspective. From statistical viewpoint, assuming that your model assumptions correspond to the data-generating model, there is nothing wrong with the unconditional (fixed effect) prediction not corresponding to the mean of the data. From a practical side, however, many people are unsatisfied with this, because they want to show predictions against data. A simple and transparent way to create marginal predictions is the simulation above: create unconditional predictions on the link scale, add random effects simulated with the estimated variances, push them through the corresponding link function and average. `emmeans` does approximately the same with `bias.adj = TRUE`, given the standard deviation of the random effects (its confidence intervals ignore the uncertainty of this standard deviation), here for the `cbpp` data of the lme4 package:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(lme4)
m = glmer(cbind(incidence, size - incidence) ~ period + (1 | herd), data = cbpp, family = binomial)
sdHerd = attr(VarCorr(m)$herd, "stddev")
emmeans(m, ~ period, type = "response")                                # unconditional
emmeans(m, ~ period, type = "response", bias.adj = TRUE, sigma = sdHerd)  # marginal
```

Here, "marginal" means averaged over the random effects (for the other meanings of the word, see @tip-re-predterms); the data-averaged effect (@sec-glm-effects) averages over the observations instead, with the random effects at zero: `emmeans(m, ~ period, counterfactuals = "period", type = "response")` gives the data-averaged effect for a typical herd (here identical to the unconditional means, because the model has no covariates), and the bias adjustment is not applied to counterfactual averages. A data-averaged effect that is also marginal over the random effects can be obtained by the simulation approach above, applied to each observation.

### ANOVA and tests for GLMMs {#sec-glm-glmmtest}

The following table summarizes our recommendations for ANOVA-type questions in GLMMs, analogous to the table for linear mixed models (@tbl-re-anova). As there, the table only lists which ANOVA types each function supports; which type to use is discussed in @sec-anova-choice.

| Question | Recommended function | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| Test fixed-effect terms (ANOVA table) | `car::Anova(m)` | Wald $\chi^2$ tests, for `glmer` and `glmmTMB` models. Types II and III (`type = "II"`, `"III"`; default II). For type I, there is no single-model test with p-values (`anova(m)` of lme4 gives none, and glmmTMB has no such method); compare a sequence of nested models, each adding one term, with `anova(m1, m2, m3)` (likelihood ratio tests). Check dispersion first (@cau-glm-before). |
| ... with fewer than about 10-20 groups, or a predictor that varies only between groups | `afex::mixed(formula, data, family = ..., method = "PB")` | The Wald p-values are then too small. `afex::mixed()` computes the whole ANOVA table with p-values from a parametric bootstrap (slow; for `glmer` models; types II and III, default III; with pbkrtest 0.5.5, this fails for `glmer` models with an error, so check that it runs and otherwise use `simulateLRT()`). Alternative for single terms, also for `glmmTMB`: `DHARMa::simulateLRT(m0, m1)`, with m0 = the model without the term. |
| How much variation do fixed and random effects explain? (description, not a test) | `lme4::VarCorr(m)`, `MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(m)` | Random effects can be compared among each other by the ratios of their variances from `VarCorr()` (on the link scale). A GLMM has no residual variance on the link scale, so VPCs as for linear mixed models (@sec-re-vpc) and R^2^ values are only approximate (they use a distribution-specific residual variance, e.g. $\pi^2/3$ for the logit link); `r.squaredGLMM()` returns one row per approximation of this residual variance: "delta" (all families), "lognormal" and "trigamma" (log links; the package help recommends "trigamma" whenever available) and "theoretical" (binomial). Report "trigamma" for log links; otherwise state which row you report. |
| Test a random effect | `DHARMa::simulateLRT(m0, m1)` | m0: the same fixed effects without the random effect (`glm()` if no random effect is left) (@sec-re-simlrt). If p = 0, report p < 1/(n+1) (@sec-anova-test). |

: ANOVA-type questions for GLMMs (`glmer`, `glmmTMB`). {#tbl-glm-glmmtest}

## Take-home messages {#sec-glm-takehome}

::: callout-tip
1.  Choose the distribution from the type of response data (counts, 0/1, k/n, positive continuous, proportions), and then check the residuals of the fitted model.
2.  The estimates are on the scale of the link function. Report effects on an interpretable scale: rate ratios for log links, odds ratios for logit links, back-transformed predictions with CIs (`emmeans(..., type = "response")`), or the data-averaged effect (`counterfactuals`); say which scale and averaging you used (@sec-glm-effects).
3.  Check dispersion before you interpret p-values: with overdispersed Poisson or k/n binomial data, p-values are too small. Overdispersion is often caused by model misfit, so check the model structure first; then use a negative binomial or beta-binomial family (if needed with a dispersion model that depends on predictors), or an observation-level random effect.
4.  Many zeros do not mean zero-inflation; zero-inflation is relative to the fitted model. Compare models with and without `ziformula` instead of relying on the residual test alone.
5.  With a nonlinear link, interactions and effects depend on the scale: decide the scale from the biology before looking at the results, and judge interactions by slopes or differences on that scale. In a GLMM, predictions from the fixed effects alone (unconditional) need not match the average prediction over the random effects (marginal) or the mean of your data.
:::

## Case studies {#sec-glm-case}

::: {#case-studies}
:::

The following case studies apply the models of this chapter to real data, including residual checks and fixes for dispersion and zero-inflation problems (@sec-glm-residual). Try to solve the exercises yourself before looking at the solutions.

### Count data - owls {#sec-glm-owl}

::: {#owls}
:::

::: {#cau-glm-owls .callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise — Owls

Look at the `Owls` data set in the `glmmTMB` package (`?Owls`). We want to know whether the begging of owl nestlings (`SiblingNegotiation`, the number of calls) depends on the food treatment and on the sex of the parent. A first model is

```{r chunk_chapter5_task_3, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(glmmTMB) # for the Owls data

m1 = glm(SiblingNegotiation ~ FoodTreatment*SexParent + offset(log(BroodSize)),
         data = Owls , family = poisson)
res = simulateResiduals(m1)
plot(res)
```

The offset `log(BroodSize)` makes the expected number of calls proportional to the number of nestlings (see the log offset in @sec-glm-poisson-note).

Try to improve the model with everything we have discussed so far (offset, dispersion, zero-inflation, random effects). Hint: besides `nbinom2`, glmmTMB offers `nbinom1`, and the dispersion can depend on predictors (`dispformula`, see @sec-disp-model).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
m1 = glmmTMB::glmmTMB(SiblingNegotiation ~ FoodTreatment * SexParent
  + (1|Nest) + offset(log(BroodSize)), data = Owls , family = nbinom1,
  dispformula = ~ FoodTreatment + SexParent,
  ziformula = ~ FoodTreatment + SexParent)
summary(m1)

res = simulateResiduals(m1, plot = T)

testDispersion(m1)
testZeroInflation(m1)
```

**Using brms** (optional, requires Stan and takes several minutes)

The same model can also be fit with brms (here without dispersion and zero-inflation terms, just to show the syntax). A step-by-step Bayesian GLMM with posterior predictive checks, overdispersion and zero-inflation (in JAGS) is developed in [the chapter on GLMMs](https://florianhartig.github.io/LearningBayes/3C-GLMM.html) of @hartig2024introduction. The brms code:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(brms)
m2 = brms::brm(SiblingNegotiation ~ FoodTreatment * SexParent
  + (1|Nest) + offset(log(BroodSize)), 
  data = Owls , 
  family = negbinomial)
summary(m2)

plot(m2, ask = FALSE)
```
:::

### Continuous proportions - plant cover {#sec-glm-cover}

Plant cover is one of the most common continuous proportions in ecology, and it comes with some special issues [@damgaard2019beta]:

- **How was cover measured?** Pin-point (point-intercept) data are hits out of N pins, i.e. k/n data; as plants grow in clumps, they are often overdispersed (beta-binomial). Cover classes (Braun-Blanquet, Londo, ...) are ordinal. Visual estimates in % are continuous, but often rounded to 1, 5 or 10%.
- **Zeros:** the choice between ordered and hurdle beta depends on what a zero means (@sec-glm-beta): "too little to be recorded" suits the ordered beta, "the species cannot grow there" the hurdle beta.
- **Totals:** because plants overlap and there is bare ground, the cover of all species in a plot does not sum to 100%. Only relative cover (share of total vegetation) sums to 1.
- **Several species:** the cover of species in the same plot is usually correlated (@sec-glm-shares). For joint models of many species, @korhonen2024comparison found the hurdle beta most accurate in simulations, with no noticeable difference to ordered beta for real data.

The data set `varespec` (package vegan) contains visually estimated cover (in %) of 44 species in 24 reindeer-grazed lichen pastures in Finland; `varechem` contains soil chemistry for the same plots. We ask whether the cover of heather (*Calluna vulgaris*, `Callvulg`) depends on soil aluminum. Heather is absent in 9 of the 24 plots:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(vegan)
data(varespec)
data(varechem)
# Al is scaled (per SD); [, 1] drops the attributes, so that predict() works
# with new values given in SD units, e.g. Al = c(-1, 0, 1)
d <- data.frame(cover = varespec$Callvulg / 100, Al = scale(varechem$Al)[, 1])
table(d$cover == 0)
```

A beta regression fails because of the zeros:

```{r, error=TRUE}
glmmTMB(cover ~ Al, family = beta_family, data = d)
```

A logit transform needs a constant to deal with the zeros. The result depends on this arbitrary choice:

```{r}
sapply(c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05), function(eps) {
  coef(lm(qlogis((d$cover + eps) / (1 + 2 * eps)) ~ Al, data = d))["Al"]
})
```

The ordered beta handles the zeros directly:

```{r}
m_ord <- glmmTMB(cover ~ Al, family = ordbeta(), data = d)
summary(m_ord)
plot(simulateResiduals(m_ord))
```

The hurdle beta separates presence and cover. Note that the zero part (`ziformula`) models the probability of *absence*:

```{r}
m_hurdle <- glmmTMB(cover ~ Al, ziformula = ~ Al, family = beta_family, data = d)
summary(m_hurdle)
```

The data hint that more aluminum raises the probability that heather is present (negative coefficient on absence, p = 0.10), with no sign of an effect on its cover where it is present.

For the expected cover at low, mean and high aluminum (-1, 0, 1 SD), we can use `predict()` for the hurdle model:

```{r}
newd <- data.frame(Al = c(-1, 0, 1))
predict(m_hurdle, newdata = newd, type = "response")
```

For the ordered beta, `predict(type = "response")` gives only the mean of the continuous part, ignoring the zeros; the expected cover has to be computed from the thresholds with a small helper function (see the box):

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Expected values for the ordered beta

The ordered beta has a linear predictor $\eta$ and two thresholds $\psi_1 < \psi_2$ (stored as `psi`). The probability of an exact 0 is $1 - \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta - \psi_1)$, of an exact 1 it is $\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta - \psi_2)$, and in between the values follow a beta with mean $\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta)$. The expected value combines the three parts:

```{r}
ordbeta_mean <- function(m, newdata) {
  eta <- predict(m, newdata = newdata, type = "link", re.form = NA)
  psi <- m$fit$par[names(m$fit$par) == "psi"]   # the two thresholds
  p0 <- 1 - plogis(eta - psi[1])                  # P(y = 0)
  p1 <- plogis(eta - psi[2])                      # P(y = 1)
  p1 + (1 - p0 - p1) * plogis(eta)
}
```

`re.form = NA` sets random effects to zero, so the function also works for mixed models. If the data contain no 1s, the upper threshold cannot be estimated well and gets a very large value (here about 19), which does no harm.
:::

```{r}
ordbeta_mean(m_ord, newd)
```

Both models give similar predictions; the hurdle beta additionally shows where the effect acts.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise — Bilberry

Bilberry (*Vaccinium myrtillus*, `Vaccmyrt`) is absent in 14 of the 24 plots. Analyze whether its cover depends on the depth of the humus layer (`varechem$Humdepth`). Fit an ordered beta and a hurdle beta, check the residuals, and compare the results: does humus depth act on the presence of bilberry, on its cover where present, or on both?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

```{r}
d2 <- data.frame(cover = varespec$Vaccmyrt / 100,
                 Hum = scale(varechem$Humdepth)[, 1])  # scaled, as Al above
table(d2$cover == 0)

m_ord2 <- glmmTMB(cover ~ Hum, family = ordbeta(), data = d2)
summary(m_ord2)
plot(simulateResiduals(m_ord2))

m_hur2 <- glmmTMB(cover ~ Hum, ziformula = ~ Hum, family = beta_family, data = d2)
summary(m_hur2)
plot(simulateResiduals(m_hur2))
```

The residuals of both models show no problems. The ordered beta finds a clear positive effect of humus depth. The hurdle beta shows where it acts: deeper humus lowers the probability that bilberry is absent (zero part, p = 0.02), but has no clear effect on its cover where it is present. The predicted probability of presence and the expected cover at shallow, mean and deep humus (-1, 0, 1 SD):

```{r}
newd2 <- data.frame(Hum = c(-1, 0, 1))
1 - predict(m_hur2, newdata = newd2, type = "zprob")  # probability of presence
predict(m_hur2, newdata = newd2, type = "response")   # expected cover, hurdle
ordbeta_mean(m_ord2, newd2)                           # expected cover, ordered beta
```

Both models predict that the expected cover increases with humus depth (about tenfold, but from very low values; it stays below 5%), but only the hurdle beta tells us that this is mainly because bilberry occurs more often on deep humus.
:::

### Binomial GLM - snails {#sec-glm-snail}

The following dataset contains information about the occurrences of 3 freshwater snail species and their infection rate with schistosomiasis (freshwater snails are intermediate hosts). The data and the analysis is from @rabone2019freshwater.

```{r chunk_chapter4_chunk1, echo=TRUE, eval=T}
library(EcoData)
?EcoData::snails
```

The dataset has data on three snail species: *Biomphalaria pfeifferi* (BP), *Bulinus forskalii* (BF), and *Bulinus truncatus* (BT). For this task, we will focus only on *Bulinus truncatus* (BT).

We want to answer two questions:

1.  What are the variables that explain the occurrence of the *Bulinus truncatus* species (=Species distribution model)
2.  What are the variables that influence the infection of the snails with Schistosomiasis

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise — Snails

- Build two binomial GLMs (see hints) to explain the presence and the infection rate of *Bulinus truncatus* (BT)

- Add environmental variables and potential confounders (see ?EcoData::snails for an overview of the variables and if you want, you can also take a look at the original paper)

- Check residuals with DHARMa, check for misfits (plot residuals against variables)

- Which variables explain the presence of BT and which have an effect on the infection rates?
:::

::: callout-tip
#### Hints

Prepare dataset before the analysis:

```{r}
data = EcoData::snails
data$sTemp_Water = scale(data$Temp_Water)
data$spH = scale(data$pH)
data$swater_speed_ms = scale(data$water_speed_ms)
data$swater_depth = scale(data$water_depth)
data$sCond = scale(data$Cond)
data$swmo_prec = scale(data$wmo_prec)
data$syear = scale(data$year)
data$sLat = scale(data$Latitude)
data$sLon = scale(data$Longitude)
data$sTemp_Air = scale(data$Temp_Air)
# Remove NAs
vars = c("Temp_Water", "pH", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Cond", "seas_wmo", "wmo_prec", "water_speed_ms", "water_depth", "Temp_Air", "year", "duration", "locality", "site_irn", "coll_date")
data = data[complete.cases(data[, vars]), ]
```

1.  Factors which drive the occurrence of BT

    Minimal model:

    ```{r}
    model1 = glm(bt_pres~ sTemp_Water,
                 data = data,  family = binomial)
    ```

    Add environmental variables such as Temperature, pH, water metrics (e.g. water speed etc). Which variables could be potential confounders (year? locality? Season?....)

2.  Factors which affect the infection rate

    We use a k/n binomial model:

    ```{r}
    model2 = glm(cbind(BT_pos_tot, BT_tot - BT_pos_tot )~ sTemp_Water ,
                     data = data[data$BT_tot > 0, ],  family = binomial)
    ```

    Add environmental variables such as Temperature, pH, water metrics (e.g. water speed etc). Which variables could be potential confounders (year? locality? Season?....)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

**Species distribution model**

Environmental variables (part of our hypothesis): Temp_water, Temp_Air, pH, Cond, swmo_prec, water_speed_ms, and water_depth.

Potential confounders: site_type, year, seas_wmo (season) (, and locality)

Our model:

```{r}
model1 = glm(bt_pres~ site_type + sTemp_Water + spH +
               sCond + swmo_prec + swater_speed_ms  + duration + 
               sTemp_Air + seas_wmo + syear + swater_depth,
               data = data,  family = binomial)
summary(model1)
```

Intercept corresponds to seas_wmo == dry and site_type == can.2

Coefficients of confounders (here year, site type and season) are not interpreted (Table 2 fallacy, @sec-causal-table2). We only interpret the variables of our hypothesis: conductivity has a clear positive effect, precipitation, water speed and air temperature clear negative effects. Let's look at the effects:

```{r,warning=FALSE}
plot(allEffects(model1))
```

it appears that conductivity has the largest positive effect on occurrence rates. It is reasonable to assume that there are interactions between freshwater (site_type) and factors such as conductivity:

```{r,warning=FALSE}
model1 = glm(bt_pres~ site_type * sCond -sCond + swater_speed_ms+spH + sTemp_Water + swmo_prec + duration + 
                 sTemp_Air + seas_wmo + syear + swater_depth,
             data = data,  family = binomial)
summary(model1)
```

"-sCond" allows us to test the slopes for the different site_types against 0 (no reference level)

Residual checks:

```{r}
library(DHARMa)
sim = simulateResiduals(model1, plot = TRUE)
```

Check misfits by plotting predictors against residuals:

```{r}
plotResiduals(sim, data$sCond)
plotResiduals(sim, data$sTemp_Air)
```

They look okay!

**Bonus - Spatial autocorrelation:**

A common problem with spatial data is spatial autocorrelation. We can use DHARMa to test if our residuals are spatially autocorrelated

```{r}
res2 = recalculateResiduals(sim, group = c(data$site_irn))
groupLocations = aggregate(cbind(data$sLat, data$sLon ), list( data$site_irn), mean)
testSpatialAutocorrelation(res2, x = groupLocations$V1, y = groupLocations$V2)
```

The test is significant, i.e. we should assume that the data is spatially autocorrelated. Addressing this issue, however, is covered in chapter 4C
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
#### Solution

**Infection rate**

Environmental variables (part of our hypothesis): Temp_water, Temp_Air, pH, Cond, swmo_prec, water_speed_ms, and water_depth.

Potential confounders: site_type, year, seas_wmo (season), duration, ( and locality)

Our model:

```{r}
data_inf = data[data$BT_tot > 0 , ] # only observations 

model2 = glm(cbind(BT_pos_tot, BT_tot - BT_pos_tot )~ site_type + sTemp_Water + spH +
               sCond + log(swmo_prec+1) + swater_speed_ms  + log(duration) + 
               sTemp_Air + seas_wmo + syear + swater_depth,
               data = data_inf,  family = binomial)
summary(model2)
```

Intercept corresponds to seas_wmo == dry and site_type == can.2

Again, coefficients of confounders (year, site type, season) are not interpreted (Table 2 fallacy, @sec-causal-table2). Let's look at the estimates of our hypothesis variables:

```{r,warning=FALSE}
plot(allEffects(model2))
```

With partial residuals:

```{r,warning=FALSE}
plot(allEffects(model2, partial.residuals = TRUE))
```

Reminder: The partial residuals don't tell us anything because the variance of the residuals (remember binomial) depends on the probability of the binomial process AND on k (k/n binomial model). We need DHARMa to check the residuals:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(DHARMa)
sim = simulateResiduals(model2, plot = TRUE)

```

Residuals look okayish for a k/n model.

Check misfits by plotting predictors against residuals:

```{r, message=FALSE}
plotResiduals(sim, log(data_inf$swmo_prec+1))
plotResiduals(sim, data_inf$sTemp_Water)
```

swmo_prec doesn't look good but this is caused by the many zeros in the variable
:::

### Making spatial predictions with a logistic regression - elephant SDM {#sec-glm-elephant}

To demonstrate how to fit a species distribution model and extrapolate it in space, let's have a look at the elephant dataset, which is contained in EcoData

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
library(EcoData)
?elephant
```

The object elephant contains two subdatasets

1.  elephant\$occurenceData contains presence / absence data as well as bioclim variables (environmental predictors) for the African elephant

2.  elephant\$predictionData data with environmental predictors for spatial predictions

The environmental data consists of 19 environmental variables, called bio1 through bio19, which are public and globally available bioclimatic variables (see <https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html> for a description of the variables). For example, bio1 is the mean annual temperature. No understanding of these variables is required for the task, the only difficulty is that many of them are highly correlated because they encode similar information (e.g. there are several temperature variables).

The goal of this exercise is to fit a logistic regression model based on the observed presence / absences, and then make new predictions of habitat suitability in space across Africa based on the fitted model. Thus, our workflow consists of two steps:

1.  building and optimizing the predictive model, and
2.  using the predictive model to make predictions on new data and visualizing the results.

Here an example of how you could do this

**Build predictive model:**

```{r}
model = glm(Presence~bio1, data = elephant$occurenceData, family = binomial()) # minimum model
```

To check the predictive power of the model, you can either use

```{r, message=F}
AIC(model) 
library(pROC)
auc(elephant$occurenceData$Presence, predict(model, type = "response"))
```

The AUC is a common measure of how well a model separates presences from absences: the probability that a randomly chosen presence gets a higher predicted value than a randomly chosen absence (0.5 = random, 1 = perfect). However, it doesn't penalize for complexity, as the AIC. Better to look at it under cross-validation. As explained in the section on cross-validation (@sec-select-cv), we collect the out-of-sample predictions of all folds and calculate the AUC once. Because the loop uses `update()`, it works for any model you fit to these data:

```{r}
dat = elephant$occurenceData
set.seed(123)
fold = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(dat)))  # random assignment to 5 folds
predCV = numeric(nrow(dat))
for (k in 1:5) {
  fit = update(model, data = dat[fold != k, ])
  predCV[fold == k] = predict(fit, newdata = dat[fold == k, ], type = "response")
}
auc(dat$Presence, predCV)
```

Currently, fit and validation AUC are nearly identical (0.71), because we have a very simple model. However, for more complex models, this could change.

- Drop some of the highly correlated variables (don't use all of them).

- Use quadratic effects

- Use `stepAIC` or the `dredge` function (@tip-select-stepwise) to optimize the predictive model

**Make new predictions**

The data for making spatial predictions is in elephant\$predictionData. This new dataset is not a data.frame but a raster object, which is a special data class for spatial data. You can plot one of the predictors in the following way.

```{r, message = F}
library(sp)
library(raster)
plot(elephant$predictionData$bio1)
```

As our new_data object is not a typical data.frame, we are not using the standard predict function for a glm, which is ?predict.glm, but the predict function from the raster object (which internally transforms the new_data into a classical data.frame, pass then the data.frame to our model, and then transforms the output back to a raster object). Therefore, the syntax is slightly different to how we previously used predict().

```{r}
predictions =  predict(elephant$predictionData, model = model, type = "response")
head(as.data.frame(predictions))
```

The advantage of the raster object is that we can directly use it to create a map (the raster object has coordinates for each observation):

```{r}
spplot(predictions, colorkey = list(space = "left") )
```

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
#### Exercise

Play around with the logistic regression to improve predictive accuracy. You can check predictive accuracy by looking at AIC or by taking out a bit of the data for validation, e.g. by AUC. When improving the predictive power of the model, does the map change?
:::
